## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Advanced Graph Neural Networks
  Code                    Not communicated — module announced by the master's brochure; SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet not published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).
  Team and workload       LLGA team (École Polytechnique) · teaching hours and ECTS not communicated · the “research” continuation of the Graph ML module (M1 P2): expressive power and the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, over-squashing, positional encodings, graph transformers, temporal GNNs, robustness — up to industrial scale and the laboratory's research.
  Period                  M2 · period 1 (announced)
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2} M2 program being finalized by the course instructors; official description not communicated until the sheet is published.
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who has already trained a GCN or a GAT (M1 Graph ML) and has seen accuracy stall with depth, or two different molecules receive identical scores. **Empirical first**: we start from what fails in practice — information that does not get through a bottleneck, a GNN that cannot separate two regular graphs — and only then name the concepts that explain it: expressive power, positional encodings, graph transformers.

The module is the research follow-up to M1 Graph ML: the Weisfeiler-Lehman test, over-squashing, positional encodings, graph transformers, temporal graphs, scale and robustness. The official sheet is not published; these notes develop the themes announced by the brochure and flag what they add.

### What you will be able to do

-   Determine the expressive power of a GNN via the Weisfeiler-Lehman test and deduce what it cannot distinguish.
-   Diagnose over-squashing in deep GNNs and choose the appropriate remedies.
-   Choose a positional or structural encoding depending on the task and the graph.
-   Decide between a message passing GNN and a graph transformer, and justify the choice.
-   Handle dynamic and temporal graphs.
-   Scale a GNN: sampling, systems and trade-offs.
-   Analyze the robustness and privacy specific to relational data.
-   Situate the open bridges: 3D, algorithmic reasoning, GNN × LLM.

### Where this course fits in the program

An M2 module (period 1), whose official teaching volume is not communicated. It builds directly on the message passing foundation of [Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html) (M1 P2), reactivated in chapter 0. Downstream, it prepares [Graph Generative Models and Applications](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html), which builds graphs rather than analyzing them, and [Fundamentals of Security and Robustness for AI](../m2-security-robustness/index.html) (M2 P2), which recaps Nettack in one case study and a lab and takes the robustness chapter (ch. 7), where Nettack, its successors and the defenses are developed, as optional upstream reading.

### Course outline

-   **Background: the message passing foundation** — the M1 base GNN restated, to expose its limits.
-   **Scale: sampling, systems** — making training fit on industrial graphs, and the experimental hygiene used in every later chapter.
-   **Expressive power: the Weisfeiler-Lehman test** — the exact bound of what a standard GNN can distinguish.
-   **Over-squashing and deep GNNs** — why information compresses poorly in deep architectures, and how to remedy it.
-   **Positional and structural encodings** — giving the graph what transformers have beyond message passing.
-   **Graph transformers** — attention applied to vertices: promises, costs and conditions of use.
-   **Dynamic and temporal graphs** — handling structures that evolve over time.
-   **Robustness and privacy on graphs** — attacking and defending models whose data is relational.
-   **LLGA bridges: 3D, algorithmic reasoning, GNN × LLM** — where this research meets the master's other axes.
-   **Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Lutzeyer)** — the laboratory's papers, read with the module's grid (self-study).
-   **Exercises** — expressiveness tests, encodings and scaling to carry out yourself.
-   **Projects and assessment** — solo and group project subjects, a mock written exam and a grading rubric (proposals).
-   **References** — the research papers underlying each chapter.

### How to study this module

-   First secure the foundation: the review chapter 0 conditions everything else in the module.
-   Implement the Weisfeiler-Lehman test on small graphs: nothing makes expressive power as concrete as two indistinguishable graphs.
-   Read each founding paper after the corresponding chapter: the course is its map, not its substitute.
-   Treat the robustness chapter (ch. 7) as the place where Nettack, its successors and the graph defenses are studied for their own sake; the M2 P2 security module only recaps Nettack (case study 9.2 and a lab) and lists ch. 7 as useful if taken.
-   Experiment with scaling on large datasets, and measure what sampling costs in quality.
-   Explore the bridges of chapter 8 and the research of chapter 9: this is where internship and PhD topics are recruited.

::: note
[independent note]{.tag} This module carries the graph half of the master up to the GNN × LLM crossroads. Whether you aim at research (PhD, research engineer) or at large-scale industrial GNNs, the habit to acquire is the same: diagnose expressive power and over-squashing before stacking layers.
:::

## 0. Background: the message passing foundation {#ch0}

This chapter restates the M1 message passing GNN and the facts about it that the module assumes; its last item, over-smoothing, is the first of the limits that the following chapters study.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Review of the Graph ML module (M1 P2) — what is assumed known
:::

-   **Generic layer** (M1, ch. 5):
    $$
    h_v^{(\ell+1)} = \phi\big(h_v, \mathrm{AGG}_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)}\{\psi(h_v, h_u)\}\big) ;
    $$
    GCN (renormalized averaging, spectral derivation), GraphSAGE (sampling, inductive), GAT (edge attention);
-   **Spectral** (M1, ch. 4): Laplacian $L = D - A$, variational characterization of $\lambda_2$, spectral clustering as a RatioCut relaxation, convolution by Chebyshev polynomials — filtering = a polynomial of $L$;
-   **Embeddings** (M1, ch. 3): DeepWalk/node2vec and their NetMF reading (factorization of random-walk matrices); the PathNNs of ch. 9 are their generalization;
-   **Link prediction / GAE** (M1, ch. 6) and **scale** (M1, ch. 7: NeighborSampler, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAINT) — the ch. 1 below extends the latter;
-   **Over-smoothing** (M1, ch. 5): after many layers, all embeddings converge (proved on a regular graph: geometric convergence to the mean) — why one stops at 2-4 layers… and why this module exists.
-   **Notation** (the site-wide convention, as in [Graph ML ch. 0](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch0)):
    $$
    \tilde A = A + I, \quad \hat A = \tilde D^{-1/2} \tilde A \tilde D^{-1/2}, \quad P = D^{-1} A, \quad L = D - A, \quad L_{\mathrm{sym}} = I - D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2} .
    $$
    $\hat A$ is the GCN propagator and $P$ the random walk, nothing else. Laplacian eigenvalues are listed in ascending order, $0 = \lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots$, so $\lambda_2$ is the spectral gap. Node features are rows, so a layer reads $H W$.
::::

::: note
[The module's four research questions]{.tag} (1) *How far can a GNN see?* — expressive power (ch. 2); (2) *How far can information travel?* — over-squashing and depth (ch. 3); (3) *Where am I in the graph?* — position and structure (ch. 4); (4) *At what scale and under what attacks?* — systems (ch. 1) and robustness (ch. 7). Transformers (ch. 5) and the temporal dimension (ch. 6) answer "all-all" and "as time goes by" to these same questions.
:::

## 1. Scale: sampling, systems {#ch1}

Real graphs have millions of nodes, and a careless experiment can make a method look better than it is. This chapter covers the systems side of training at scale and the experimental protocol (seeds, confidence intervals, leakage checks) that every later chapter relies on.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
What is assumed known (M1, ch. 7)
:::

NeighborSampler (fanouts, expansive neighborhood $1 + s_L(1 + s_{L-1}(\dots))$), Cluster-GCN (METIS partitioning, partition bias), GraphSAINT (subgraphs + bias-free coverage normalization), and the bias/variance/memory triangle. Here: the *systems* layer and experimental hygiene.
::::

-   **Multi-GPU and partitioning**: beyond one GPU, partition the graph (METIS/vertex-cut) across several machines; boundary edges are duplicated (shadow nodes) — the distributed training of the Emerging ML module applies almost as is (parameter server vs all-reduce); PinSage (M1, ch. 6) is the industrial reference;
-   **Caching and pipelining**: neighborhood sampling is a *system* problem (I/O, reuse of subgraphs across batches — hence PinSage's importance sampling that freezes the entry points); the frameworks: DGL, PyG + torch_geometric.sampler, Quiver;
-   **Summary of complexities**:
      Method            Memory/batch                          Bias        Notes
      ----------------- ------------------------------------- ----------- --------------------------
      full-batch        $\mathcal{O}(|V| + |E|)$              none        breaks beyond \~1M nodes
      NeighborSampler   $\mathcal{O}(\prod s_l)$              variance    inductive, standard
      Cluster-GCN       $\mathcal{O}(|E|/k)$                  partition   deep possible
      GraphSAINT        $\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{G}_s|)$        corrected   dense batches
-   **Benchmarks and hygiene**: OGB (ogbn-arxiv 169k; ogbn-products 2.4M; PCQM4M 3.7M molecules), public leaderboards; the "Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks" paper (Dwivedi et al., 2020/2023) sets the protocol: same parameter budgets, same splits, *multiple seeds with confidence intervals* — many "SOTAs" die by this yardstick; Bayesian hyperparameter search is the rule (gains < 0.5 point demanding a strict protocol);
-   **Good research practice**: always publish the variance, test significance (paired tests over seeds), and check for *leakage* (temporal splits for dynamic graphs — ch. 6).

## 2. Expressive power: the Weisfeiler-Lehman test {#ch2}

Which graphs can a message passing GNN tell apart, and which ones will it always confuse? This chapter answers exactly, with the Weisfeiler-Lehman test. A concrete scene: take two non-isomorphic 6-regular graphs. Your 3-layer GCN produces the same embeddings for both (up to permutation), and a link-prediction AUC around 0.5. This is not an implementation bug but the 1-WL bound, which this chapter makes operational *before* any architectural gadget is added.

The statement of this bound and of the GIN result is already in [Graph ML, Proposition 5.1b](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5). Here we prove both, then go beyond 1-WL.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three classic mistakes: believing that a deeper GNN "sees more" (often false); evaluating only on graphs that 1-WL already separates (which gives a false sense of power); and ignoring the initial features (they fix the initial colors). All three mislead the reading of papers as much as a small molecular experiment.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — 1-WL (color refinement)]{.tag} Initialize a color $c_v^{(0)}$ from the features; iterate:
$$
c_v^{(k+1)} = \mathrm{HASH}\Big(c_v^{(k)},\ \mathrm{SORT}\big\{c_u^{(k)} : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\big\}\Big).
$$
Two graphs are *1-WL-equivalent* if the multisets of colors coincide at convergence.

1-WL distinguishes *almost all* random graphs (Babai-Erdős-Selkow); but fails on simple families: regular graphs of the same degree, cycles, pairs of molecules discussed since the 1960s (CIR: chemical identity recognition).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — GNN ≤ 1-WL (Xu et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2019)]{.tag} Any message passing GNN whose aggregation and update are functions (continuous, computable) cannot distinguish two 1-WL-equivalent graphs: if the initial colors coincide and the layers saturate the test, the embeddings coincide at every depth.

::: proof
By induction on $\ell$.

1.  *Initialization*: initial colors = features, identical by assumption, so $h_v^{(0)} = h_{v'}^{(0)}$ for every pair $(v, v')$ of the same color.
2.  *Heredity*: if all nodes of color $c$ have the same representation $h_c$, then the input of the aggregation at $v$ is the multiset $\{h_c : c \in \mathrm{multicol}_v\}$. Now 1-WL-equivalence = equality of color multisets *and* of neighbor color multisets at each iteration — so AGG receives identical inputs, and
    $$
    h_v^{(\ell+1)} = h_{v'}^{(\ell+1)} .
    $$
3.  *Readout*: in the end, the readouts (permutation-invariant by construction, M1 ch. 2) see only the multiset of the $h_v$ — identical on both graphs. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — GIN reaches exactly 1-WL (Xu et al., 2019)]{.tag} With sum + MLP and discrete features,
$$
h_v^{(k+1)} = \mathrm{MLP}^{(k)}\Big((1 + \epsilon^{(k)})\, h_v^{(k)} + \sum_{u \in \mathcal{N}(v)} h_u^{(k)}\Big)
$$
the GNN distinguishes exactly what 1-WL distinguishes.

::: proof
The ingredient: on a countable domain, there exists an *injective* function $f : \text{finite multisets} \to \mathbb{R}$. Encoding each element by an integer (canonical log of a prime: $c \mapsto \log p_c$) gives $\sum_i \log p_{c_i}$, and the uniqueness of prime factorization ensures injectivity; a universal MLP approximates it.

Then the sum+MLP layer is injective in $(h_v, \mathrm{multiset}(h_u))$ — the pair (own color, neighbor multiset) is encoded without collision. By induction, two nodes have the same embedding $\iff$ same 1-WL color. The injective sum readout concludes: GIN = 1-WL. [∎]{.qed}
:::

Immediate consequences: mean and max are *not* injective — $\{a, a, a\}$ and $\{a\}$ have the same mean; $\{a, a\}$ and $\{a\}$ the same max. So GCN/GraphSAGE (mean) are *strictly less* powerful than GIN on categorical features.

In practice the difference shows up mainly on tasks where *counting* neighbors matters (molecules: $\mathrm{CH}_4$ vs $\mathrm{CH}_3$-$\mathrm{CH}_3$).
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — C6 vs 2×C3: 1-WL fails, the folklore pair test 2-FWL separates (demonstration)]{.tag}

-   *1-WL*: all nodes have degree 2; by induction, at each round each node sees (its color, {its color, its color}). The colors remain uniform on each graph, and identical *between* the two graphs: **indistinguishable**.
-   *2-FWL* (pair coloring, "folklore" rule): consider an adjacent pair $(u, v)$. In the triangle, $\{w : w \sim u, w \sim v\}$ counts 1 common vertex; in C6, this count is 0 (no triangles). The update aggregates for the pair $(u,v)$ the multiset of *joint* colors $\big(c(u, w), c(w, v)\big)$ over all $w$. It therefore encodes the number of triangles on each edge — the pair histograms differ: **separated**. [∎]{.qed}

Moral: a pair test with the joint rule (hence a pair GNN built on it) "counts the moments" that the local sum cannot see. Aggregating the colors of $(u, w)$ and of $(w, v)$ as two *separate* multisets is not enough: that is the 2-WL of the box below, which equals 1-WL and fails here too. To code in the lab (exercises 1 and 5).
:::

::: thm
[k-WL and k-GNN hierarchy]{.tag} **k-WL** colors *k-tuples* of nodes. Two conventions coexist, so state which one you use.

-   *k-WL* (Morris, Grohe): a tuple is refined by $k$ separate multisets, one per coordinate that can be replaced. In this convention 2-WL has exactly the power of 1-WL, and the hierarchy is strict from $k = 2$ on: (k+1)-WL distinguishes pairs that k-WL confuses.
-   *k-FWL* ("folklore"): for each $w$, the $k$ tuples obtained by putting $w$ in each position are read *jointly*, as in Example 2.4. Then k-FWL = (k+1)-WL; in particular 2-FWL = 3-WL.

For $k$ of the order of $n$ the test decides isomorphism, at exponential cost. Even 2-FWL fails on strongly regular graphs with the same parameters, such as the $4 \times 4$ rook's graph and the Shrikhande graph.

The **k-GNNs** (Morris et al., 2019) implement a local, set-based variant of k-WL: messages between neighboring k-sets — memory and compute cost $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$: k = 2 practical, k = 3 reserved for small graphs (molecules). **PPGN** (Maron et al., 2019) reaches 2-FWL = 3-WL with matrix products on $n \times n$ pair tensors. Morris et al.'s survey (JMLR 2023, "Weisfeiler and Leman go Machine Learning") draws the complete map.

| Model | Power | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| GCN / GraphSAGE (mean) | < 1-WL | $\mathcal{O}(|E|)$ |
| GIN (sum+MLP) | = 1-WL (= 2-WL) | $\mathcal{O}(|E|)$ |
| PathNN (ch. 9) | SP+ and AP variants strictly > 1-WL (paths) | path enumeration, exponential in the length for AP |
| GOAT (ch. 9) | strictly > invariants (learned orders) | $\mathcal{O}(|E|)$ |
| 2-FWL = 3-WL (PPGN) | counts triangles, separates C6 from 2×C3; fails on strongly regular pairs | $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ time, $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ memory |
| 3-GNN (Morris, local) | above 1-WL: a 3-set is typed by its induced subgraph, so triangles are seen | $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ |
:::

::: thm
[Pragmatic alternatives: subgraphs and motif counting]{.tag}

-   **ESAN** (Equivariant Subgraph Aggregation Networks, B. Bevilacqua et al., 2022): each graph is described by a bag of subgraphs (ego-nets of each node, or "node-deletion" — the graph deprived of $v$); a shared 1-WL GNN encodes them, aggregation across subgraphs adds expressive power *without* full $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$ cost — strictly above 1-WL and, for node-based policies, no stronger than 3-WL (Frasca et al., 2022);
-   **Motif counting** (Bouritsas et al., 2020): precompute counts of isomorphic subgraphs (triangles, paths, cycles) and inject them as features — "moments matter": raising expressive power by preprocessing rather than by architecture; direct link with Example 2.4 (triangles) and with the MMDs of generative evaluation (M1, ch. 9.6);
-   **Practical limits**: more expressive power = more estimation variance and cost; on real benchmarks (Dwivedi et al., 2023), GIN vs GCN is decided by tenths — expressive power is the bottleneck only on *structural* tasks (counting, distinguishing) — cf. ch. 1.
:::

## 3. Over-squashing and deep GNNs {#ch3}

Even when a GNN could in principle tell two nodes apart, the information may never reach them: messages from far away must squeeze through a few edges. This chapter defines this over-squashing precisely, links it to the geometry and spectrum of the graph, and presents the two families of remedies — changing the graph or changing the propagation.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Over-squashing and its Jacobian bound (Alon & Yahav, 2021; Topping et al., 2022)]{.tag} Alon & Yahav named the phenomenon: a node must receive, in one fixed-size vector, information from a receptive field that grows exponentially with depth. Topping et al. made it measurable. The influence of the input feature $x_u$ of a node $u$ on the representation of a node $v$ after $\ell$ layers is the **Jacobian**
$$
\Big| \frac{\partial h_v^{(\ell)}}{\partial x_u} \Big| .
$$
There is *over-squashing* when this sensitivity is tiny for nodes $u$ that the task needs, typically because it decays exponentially with the distance $d(u, v)$.

**The bound** (Topping et al., 2022, Lemma 1). Take an MPNN whose layer is
$$
h_v^{(\ell+1)} = \phi_\ell\Big(h_v^{(\ell)}, \sum_{w} \hat A_{vw}\, \psi_\ell\big(h_v^{(\ell)}, h_w^{(\ell)}\big)\Big),
$$
with $|\nabla \phi_\ell| \leq \alpha$ and $|\nabla \psi_\ell| \leq \beta$ at every layer. If $d(u, v) = r + 1$, then
$$
\Big| \frac{\partial h_v^{(r+1)}}{\partial x_u} \Big| \leq (\alpha\beta)^{r+1} \big(\hat A^{r+1}\big)_{vu} .
$$

*Why*: by the chain rule, the Jacobian is a sum over the walks of $r+1$ steps from $u$ to $v$. Each step contributes at most $\alpha\beta$ times the weight $\hat A$ of the edge it crosses, and the weighted sum over walks is $(\hat A^{r+1})_{vu}$.

What makes the right-hand side small is the graph, not the network. Take a full binary tree rooted at $v$ and one of its leaves $u$, at depth $r + 1$. The only walk of $r + 1$ steps between them is the path itself. With self-loops, the augmented degree is 3 at the root, 4 at the inner nodes and 2 at the leaf, so, for $r \geq 1$,
$$
(\hat A^{r+1})_{vu} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3 \cdot 4}} \Big(\frac14\Big)^{r-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{4 \cdot 2}} = \frac{4^{-r}}{\sqrt 6} .
$$
The influence of one leaf decays geometrically, while the number of leaves doubles at each level. Topping et al. quote $2^{-1}\,3^{-r}$: the same path weighted by the walk matrix $P = D^{-1}A$ instead of $\hat A$. *Bottlenecks* (bridges between communities) are where the walk weight is lost.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 3.2 — Bottleneck ⇔ small Cheeger constant ⇔ small spectral gap]{.tag} For a set $S$ of nodes, let $\partial S$ be the set of edges leaving $S$ and $\mathrm{vol}(S) = \sum_{v \in S} d_v$. The **Cheeger constant**
$$
h_G = \min_{S \neq \emptyset,\ \mathrm{vol}(S) \leq \mathrm{vol}(V)/2} \frac{|\partial S|}{\mathrm{vol}(S)}
$$
is small exactly when two large parts of the graph are joined by few edges: a bottleneck. The **Cheeger inequality** ties it to the spectral gap $\lambda_2$ of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$:
$$
\frac{\lambda_2}{2} \leq h_G \leq \sqrt{2 \lambda_2} .
$$

So *topological bottleneck ⇔ small $\lambda_2$*: the bottom of the spectrum, not its top, carries the diagnosis. Every message between the two sides crosses the few edges of $\partial S$, and the walk weights of the bound above are small there.

*Worked example*: two triangles $\{0,1,2\}$ and $\{3,4,5\}$ joined by the bridge $(2,3)$. The cut around one triangle gives
$$
h_G = \frac{1}{2 + 2 + 3} = \frac17, \qquad \lambda_2 \approx 0.205 \leq \frac27 .
$$
Adding the single edge $(1,4)$ across the bridge gives $h_G = \frac28 = \frac14$ and
$$
\lambda_2 = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt 3} \approx 0.423 :
$$
one well-placed edge doubles the gap.

Hence the two families of remedies: change the *topology* (rewiring, below) or change the *propagation* (3.4).
:::

::: thm
[3.3 — Discrete Ricci curvature and SDRF (Topping et al., 2022)]{.tag} The **Ollivier-Ricci curvature** of an edge $(u,v)$ compares neighborhoods by optimal transport:
$$
\kappa(u, v) = 1 - \frac{W_1(\mu_u, \mu_v)}{d(u, v)}, \qquad \mu_u = \text{uniform law on } \mathcal{N}(u),
$$
$W_1$ = Wasserstein-1 distance (Optimal Transport module): "locally dense" edges (triangles) → large $\kappa$; bridges → negative $\kappa$.

**Worked example** (by hand):

-   edge of a triangle: $\mu_u = \{\frac12 v, \frac12 w\}$, $\mu_v = \{\frac12 u, \frac12 w\}$; transport plan: keep $w$ (cost 0), transport $\frac12$ from $v$ to $u$ (cost 1) →
    $$
    W_1 = \frac12, \qquad \kappa = +\frac12 ;
    $$
-   edge of a hexagon C6: the best plan transports $v \to t$, $s \to u$ (cost 1 each) →
    $$
    W_1 = 1, \qquad \kappa = 0 ;
    $$
-   bridge edge between two triangles (barbell): the best plan pays
    $$
    W_1 = \frac{1}{3}(1 + 1 + 3) = \frac53 ,
    $$
    so $\kappa = -\frac23 < 0$ — the bridge is "hyperbolic": it is the bottleneck.

Topping et al. prove that negatively curved edges are those responsible for over-squashing. Conversely, if every edge has curvature at least $\kappa_0 > 0$, then $h_G \geq \kappa_0/2$ (their Proposition 5): positive curvature everywhere forbids a bottleneck.

**SDRF** (Stochastic Discrete Ricci Flow) uses Topping et al.'s **Balanced Forman curvature**, a combinatorial curvature computed from the degrees of the two endpoints and the triangles and 4-cycles through the edge — much cheaper than a transport problem. Like $\kappa$, it is positive on triangle edges, zero on the edges of C6 and $-\frac23$ on the barbell bridge. At each iteration:

1.  take the edge $(i, j)$ of minimal curvature;
2.  for each candidate edge $(k, l)$ not yet present, with $k$ equal or adjacent to $i$ and $l$ equal or adjacent to $j$, compute how much adding it would raise the curvature of $(i, j)$; *sample* one candidate with a softmax of these improvements (a temperature sets how greedy the choice is) and add it — this creates a triangle or a 4-cycle around the bottleneck;
3.  remove the edge of maximal curvature if it exceeds a threshold (avoid densification).

Effect: the most negative curvatures rise, the bottleneck widens, and $h_G$ and $\lambda_2$ typically increase — the edge $(1,4)$ of the worked example of Proposition 3.2 is exactly such an addition. *Looking at the graph as a geometric object* — curvatures, distances, volumes — is one of the field's great turns (cf. ch. 8 and the Geometric DL module).
:::

::: note
[DIGL — diffusion rewiring (Gasteiger, Weißenberger & Günnemann, NeurIPS 2019)]{.tag} A "filtering" alternative: replace $A$ by a sparsified *generalized graph diffusion*
$$
S = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \theta_k\, T^k ,
$$
with $T$ a transition matrix of the graph (a random walk, possibly symmetrically normalized). Two classical choices of weights are personalized PageRank, $\theta_k = \alpha(1-\alpha)^k$, and the heat kernel, $\theta_k = e^{-t} t^k / k!$. $S$ is then sparsified (top-$k$ entries per column, or a threshold $\varepsilon$). Each node gains "virtual" edges toward its multihop neighbors weighted by the diffusion; simple, and the final GNN trains on the *rewired* graph.

Comparison: SDRF is *topological* (local curvature, targeted additions); DIGL is *spectral* (global diffusion). Diffusion scores across a bottleneck are small, so top-$k$ sparsification keeps mostly edges *inside* communities: Topping et al. (Theorem 6) show that after PPR rewiring the Cheeger ratio of a cut stays below a fixed multiple of its old value, a factor set by $\alpha$ and the degrees: a narrow bottleneck stays narrow. DIGL therefore helps on homophilous graphs more than against over-squashing. Both may destroy motif information: measure the trade-off in the lab (exercise 6).
:::

::: thm
[3.4 — Deep GNNs: APPNP and GCNII]{.tag} **APPNP** (Klicpera et al., 2019) separates *predicting* from *propagating*: a network (often simple) predicts $H = f_\theta(X)$; propagation follows personalized PageRank with the GCN propagator $\hat A$ of ch. 0:
$$
Z^{(k+1)} = (1 - \alpha)\, \hat A\, Z^{(k)} + \alpha H .
$$
Fixed point:
$$
Z^* = \alpha \big(I - (1 - \alpha)\hat A\big)^{-1} H .
$$
The series expansion $\sum_{k} \alpha(1-\alpha)^k \hat A^k$ shows that the effective depth is *infinite* without stacking parameters. Here $\alpha$ is the PageRank teleport probability of [Graph ML Definition 0.9](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch0): the restart term $\alpha H$ keeps every node anchored to its own prediction and kills over-smoothing (M1, ch. 5.3); $K$ iterations = truncation of the series.

**GCNII** (Chen et al., 2020) makes GCN *truly* deep through two mechanisms:
$$
H^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\Big( \big[(1-\alpha_\ell)\, \hat A H^{(\ell)} + \alpha_\ell H^{(0)}\big]\big[(1-\beta_\ell) I + \beta_\ell W^{(\ell)}\big] \Big)
$$

-   *initial residual*: the propagated $\hat A H^{(\ell)}$ is mixed with the first layer $H^{(0)}$ itself, not propagated — $\alpha_\ell$ plays the role of APPNP's teleport (typically $\alpha_\ell = 0.1$);
-   *identity mapping*: the weight matrix is pulled toward the identity, as in ResNet, with
    $$
    \beta_\ell = \log\Big(\frac{\lambda}{\ell} + 1\Big) \approx \frac{\lambda}{\ell} ,
    $$
    where $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter, not an eigenvalue (the paper uses 0.5 on the citation graphs and 1.0 on PPI). $\beta_\ell$ *decreases* with depth: deep layers are close to the identity, so stacking them does not degrade the representation. With these two mechanisms, GCNII trains up to 64 layers.

Positioning: rewiring (3.3) changes *the channel*; APPNP/GCNII change *the dynamics*; graph transformers (ch. 5) remove the bottleneck by making the channel all-all; over-smoothing (representation) and over-squashing (channel) remain two distinct limits that must be diagnosed separately.
:::

## 4. Positional and structural encodings {#ch4}

A GNN only sees the neighborhood of a node, not where the node sits in the whole graph. This chapter shows how to add this information as positional or structural encodings, and how to do it without breaking the invariances a GNN must respect.

::: def
[Problem: GNNs "do not know where they are"]{.tag} Message passing is equivariant (M1, ch. 2): two nodes with isomorphic neighborhoods have the same embedding — correct… but insufficient: the *global position* (distance to the center, membership in a cycle, bridge role) is informative. Transformers had the same problem (token order) and solved it with positional encodings — we re-import the idea (and its pathologies).
:::

  Encoding              Principle                                 Notes
  --------------------- ----------------------------------------- --------------------------------------------------
  **LapEig**            eigenvectors of $L$                       graph Fourier (M1, ch. 4); sign/base ambiguities
  **RWPE / RWSE**       return probabilities of the walk          simple, robust, computed by hand below
  **SE(3)-invariant**   distances, angles, areas (3D molecules)   ch. 8; Geometric DL module
  Learned / *anchor*    distances to anchor nodes                 inductive — recommended in production

::: thm
[4.1 — LapEig: the ambiguities, and SignNet to lift them]{.tag} Taking $p_v = [u_2(v), \dots, u_k(v)]$ (coordinates of $v$ on the eigenvectors) suffers from three pathologies:

1.  *sign*: $-u_i$ is also an eigenvector — two runs give opposite encodings;
2.  *basis*: if $\lambda_i$ is multiple, any rotation of the basis is admissible;
3.  *instability*: a small perturbation of the graph crosses the eigenvalues and makes the basis jump.

**SignNet** (D. Lim et al., 2023) builds functions invariant to the sign of each eigenvector:
$$
f(v_1, \dots, v_k) = \rho\Big( \big[\phi(v_i) + \phi(-v_i)\big]_{i=1}^{k} \Big),
$$
where $[\cdot]_i$ is a concatenation and $\phi, \rho$ are permutation-equivariant networks (for instance a GIN on the graph, with $v_i$ as node feature). Each term $\phi(v) + \phi(-v)$ is even, which gives sign invariance; the eigenvectors stay in their eigenvalue order.

Rotations inside a repeated eigenspace (pathology 2) are *not* handled by SignNet. For them, Lim et al. propose **BasisNet**, which reads each eigenspace through its projector $V_i V_i^\top$, a matrix that does not depend on the chosen basis.

The completeness result: a continuous function $h$ is sign invariant if and only if $h(v) = \phi(v) + \phi(-v)$ for some continuous $\phi$, so SignNet can represent every sign-invariant function. This mirrors the sum decomposition of Deep Sets (Zaheer et al., 2017) for multisets, the idea behind the injective sum of Theorem 2.3. In practice: LapEig + SignNet is the default PE of spectral graph transformers.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.2 — RWPE computed by hand (and why it matters)]{.tag} The *random-walk positional encoding* (RWPE, Dwivedi et al., ICLR 2022; called RWSE in GPS) of a node $v$ is the vector of return probabilities
$$
\big[ (P)_{vv}, (P^2)_{vv}, \dots, (P^K)_{vv} \big], \qquad P = D^{-1} A.
$$
Computation:

-   node of a triangle: the back-and-forths give
    $$
    (P^2)_{vv} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2} = \frac12 ,
    $$
    and going around the triangle, in both directions, gives
    $$
    (P^3)_{vv} = 2 \times (\frac12)^3 = \frac14 ;
    $$
-   node of a hexagon C6: $(P^2)_{vv} = \frac12$ — *identical* (same back-and-forths); but $(P^3)_{vv} = 0$: a return of odd length requires an odd cycle, and C6 has none. At $k = 6$, every closed walk counts, not only the two full tours: a walk of 6 steps $\pm 1$ returns when it makes 0, 3 or 6 steps forward, so
    $$
    (P^6)_{vv} = \frac{\binom{6}{0} + \binom{6}{3} + \binom{6}{6}}{2^6} = \frac{22}{64} = \frac{11}{32} ,
    $$
    the same value as for a node of the triangle, which also has 22 closed walks of length 6: only the odd lengths separate them.

Now C3 and C6 are exactly the pair that 1-WL cannot distinguish (Example 2.4). The RWSE — a single scalar, $p_3$, suffices here ($\frac14$ versus $0$) — separates them *immediately*.

Structural PEs "buy" expressive power at cost $\mathcal{O}(|E| K)$; this is why the winning models of positional benchmarks (ch. 5) systematically carry a PE.
:::

::: thm
[4.3 — SE(3) invariants for molecules, and the theory of positions]{.tag} In 3D (ch. 8), the encoding must respect rotations/translations/reflections: invariants = interatomic distances $\|x_i - x_j\|$, angles, dihedrals; it is the continuous version of the principle "use only what is invariant".

The theoretical question: *how many* coordinates to inject without breaking isomorphism invariance? A perfect positional encoding should distinguish the nodes of a *regular* graph (where 1-WL is constant) while remaining invariant under automorphism — *canonical* encodings (canonical numbering) make the learning variance explode; the practical compromise: *relative* encodings (RWSE, anchor distances, the SPD bias of ch. 5) — never absolute coordinates.
:::

::: note
[The inductive vs expressive debate]{.tag} Positional encodings partially "break" equivariance — a delicate choice between positional information and invariance guarantees. In industry (evolving graphs), one favors *inductive* PEs (generalizable to new nodes/graphs — RWSE, anchoring); in chemistry, exact invariants dominate. Cross-reference: Graphormer's SPD bias (ch. 5) is a *relative* PE — the only category that survives both constraints.
:::

## 5. Graph transformers {#ch5}

Attention lets every node exchange information with every other node in one step, which removes bottlenecks but forgets the graph. This chapter shows how graph transformers put the structure back into attention, what they cost, and when a plain message passing GNN is enough.

::: def
[Idea: all-all attention + structural bias]{.tag} Global attention $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ removes bottlenecks and over-squashing at once (ch. 3); but without an encoding of the graph, a transformer on features alone is *blind to structure*: the topology must be reinjected via (i) positional encodings (ch. 4) and (ii) additive *attention biases* in the scores — structure steers attention rather than masking it.
:::

::: thm
[5.1 — Graphormer (Ying et al., 2021) — the three structural encoders]{.tag}

1.  **centrality encoding**: an embedding of the degree (in/out if directed) added to the features — degree is the first "where am I";
2.  **spatial encoding**: a bias learned per shortest-path distance:
    $$
    \mathrm{Attention}(Q, K)_{ij} = \frac{q_i^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d}} + b_{\phi(d_{ij})}, \qquad d_{ij} = \mathrm{SPD}(i, j), \quad b_{\phi(\cdot)} \text{ learned (table)},
    $$
    with a dedicated value for $d_{ij} = \infty$ (disconnected nodes); the bias is *additive before the softmax* — structure conditions attention;
3.  **edge encoding**: on the shortest path $i \rightsquigarrow j$, the mean of the embeddings of the crossed edges is added to the score — for molecules, the type of the bonds along the path matters.

Plus a global virtual node (connected to all) for the readout. Result: 1^st^ rank on OGB-LSC PCQM4M (3.7M molecules) at its release. Implementation:

```python
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn
from scipy.sparse.csgraph import shortest_path

def spd_matrix(adj):                                 # adj: (n, n) 0/1 NumPy array
    d = shortest_path(adj, unweighted=True)          # BFS from every node; inf if unreachable
    d[np.isinf(d)] = -1                              # -1 marks "unreachable"
    return torch.as_tensor(d, dtype=torch.long)

class GraphormerLayer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, h, max_spd=5):
        super().__init__()
        self.max_spd = max_spd
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d, h, batch_first=True)
        self.bias = nn.Embedding(max_spd + 2, h)     # b_phi: 0..max_spd, plus one slot for "unreachable"
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 2*d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(2*d, d))
    def forward(self, x, spd):                       # x: (1, n, d), one graph; spd: from spd_matrix
        idx = spd.clamp(max=self.max_spd)            # long distances share the last slot
        idx = torch.where(spd < 0, torch.full_like(spd, self.max_spd + 1), idx)
        b = self.bias(idx).permute(2, 0, 1)          # (h, n, n) = (batch * heads, n, n) for a batch of 1
        x = self.attn(x, x, x, attn_mask=b)[0] + x   # a float attn_mask is added to the scores
        return self.ffn(x) + x
```

*Two details*: `nn.MultiheadAttention` takes the additive bias as a float `attn_mask` of shape (batch · heads, n, n); and the dedicated slot `max_spd + 1` keeps disconnected pairs apart from distant ones. The per-head bias is an embedding table indexed by the distance matrix (exercise 7).
:::

::: thm
[5.2 — GPS (Rampasek et al., 2022): the two channels, layer by layer]{.tag}
$$
H^{(\ell+1)} = \mathrm{MLP}\Big( \mathrm{BN}\big(\underbrace{\mathrm{MSA}(H^{(\ell)} + \mathrm{PE})}_{\text{global channel}} \;+\; \underbrace{\mathrm{MPNN}(H^{(\ell)}, A)}_{\text{local channel}}\big) \Big)
$$
— *global* attention (all-all; kills over-squashing) + *local* message passing (locality bias, convolution); PE injected at the input (ch. 4); graph batches by concatenation-padding.

Per-layer complexity: $\mathcal{O}(n^2 d)$ (attention) + $\mathcal{O}(|E| d)$ (MPNN) — the global channel dominates. GPS is a *recipe*: any MPNN (GCN, GINE, GAT) and any PE (RWSE, LapEig+SignNet) plug into it — hence its status as the reference framework.
:::

::: note
[5.3 — Efficient transformers: Exphormer and sampled attention]{.tag} For large $n$ (ogbn-products…), $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ no longer fits; **Exphormer** (Shirzad et al., 2023) replaces full attention with a *sparse attention graph*:

1.  the edges of the real graph;
2.  the neighbors of a random $d$-regular **expander graph** — an expander has a spectral gap bounded away from zero and a logarithmic diameter: information crosses the graph in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ layers, precisely what ch. 3 demands (no bottleneck, by Proposition 3.2);
3.  global virtual nodes.

Complexity linear in $n + |E|$; combined with the local MPNN, this gives "Exphormer-GPS", the scalable state of the art.

Generalization: *sampled attention* (neighborhood, kernels, hashing) — the same recipes as the long-context transformers of the M2 LLMs module, transposed: the graph transformer and the LLM live the same algorithmic life.
:::

::: note
[5.4 — When is an MPNN enough? (decision guide)]{.tag}

-   *homophilous* graph, local dependencies (Cora, transactional fraud): GCN/GAT 2-3 layers — no point paying $n^2$;
-   motifs, distances, long-range dependencies (molecules, QA over KGs): transformer or ESAN (ch. 2) — structure exceeds the neighborhood;
-   large $n$: MPNN + sampling (ch. 1) or Exphormer;
-   empirical benchmark rule (Dwivedi et al., 2023): at equal size, the gain of the transformer over MPNN+PE is real but modest — the hybrid (GPS) wins most often; the PE is the dominant factor, the architecture second.

LLGA connection: "attention = complete dynamic graph" versus "GNN = attention on a given graph" (M1, ch. 5); Graphormer is the synthesis — a *given* *and* learned attention — the transformers ↔ GNN convergence is THE guiding thread of the master.
:::

## 6. Dynamic and temporal graphs {#ch6}

Many graphs change over time — transactions, edits, interactions — and the order of events carries the signal. This chapter presents the two ways of representing such graphs and the two reference architectures, TGAT and TGN.

::: def
[Two formalisms: snapshots vs event-based]{.tag}

-   **snapshots**: $G_1, G_2, \dots, G_T$ (graph aggregated per window); models: GCN+RNN (encode each snapshot, make recurrent); simple, but the granularity loses the order *within* the window;
-   **event-based**: the stream of timestamped interactions $(u, v, t_1), (u, w, t_2), \dots$ — the "true" formulation of the problem; it is the regime of fraud (millisecond) and sequential recommendation.
:::

::: thm
[6.1 — TGAT (Xu et al., 2020): encoding time]{.tag} Event-based models predate it (JODIE and DyRep, 2019, keep a recurrent state per node); TGAT injects time into attention: a learned sinusoidal temporal encoding (in the spirit of Time2Vec)
$$
\phi(\Delta t) = \big[\cos(\omega_1 \Delta t), \sin(\omega_1 \Delta t), \dots, \cos(\omega_d \Delta t), \sin(\omega_d \Delta t)\big], \qquad \omega_i \text{ learned},
$$
concatenated with the features. Attention is computed over the *strictly past* neighborhood
$$
\mathcal{N}(v; t) = \{u : (u, v, t') \in E,\ t' < t\}
$$
— a causal GAT; inductive by construction (new nodes = new times).
:::

::: thm
[6.2 — TGN (Rossi et al., 2020): the modules and their equations]{.tag} TGN factorizes temporal memory:

1.  **memory** $s_i(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$: a recurrent state per node, summarizing its history;
2.  **message**: at each event $(i, j, t)$,
    $$
    m_i^t = \mathrm{msg}(s_i(t^-), s_j(t^-), \Delta t, e_{ij})
    $$
    (likewise for $j$, symmetric);
3.  **update**:
    $$
    s_i(t) = \mathrm{GRU}\big(s_i(t^-),\ \mathrm{agg}(\{m_i^{t'} : t' \leq t\})\big)
    $$
    — only the nodes *touched by the batch* are updated; the memory of a node without events stays as it is, and its staleness is compensated by the embedding module below, which reads the memories of its neighbors;
4.  **embedding**: $z_i(t)$ computed by a TGAT-type module over the memory $\{s_u(t^-) : u \in \mathcal{N}(i; t)\}$ + the time encoding $\phi$ — memory is a *compressed summary*, the embedding an *attentive reading*.

Training: *strictly causal* — batches are ordered by time. If the memory were updated with the events of the current batch before predicting them, the model would see the answers. TGN therefore keeps a *raw message store*: for each batch, the memory is first updated with the raw messages stored from *previous* batches, then the embeddings predict the current interactions, and finally the raw messages of the current batch are stored for the next one. The memory-related modules (message function, aggregator, GRU) thus receive a gradient without leakage.

Future link prediction loss: score $(i, j, t)$ against negatives (M1, ch. 6, temporal version). The paper's ablation (Wikipedia): removing the memory costs nearly 4 points of average precision, and replacing the graph embedding module by the node's own memory (TGN-id) loses by a large margin — both the long-term memory and the attentive reading of the neighbors matter.
:::

::: note
[6.3 — LLGA application: real-time fraud]{.tag} The transaction graph is event-based by nature: a fraudulent card must be blocked in seconds. The pipeline:

1.  TGN encodes the accounts (memory = past behavior);
2.  a head classifier reads $z_i(t)$ at the moment of the transaction;
3.  the *negatives* are old legitimate transactions — beware temporal contamination (train strictly before $t$: the temporal-split protocol of [Graph ML 5.6–5.8](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5), with its worked leakage example);
4.  in production: incremental memory update, model drift to monitor.

Lab datasets: Wikipedia edits / Reddit (TGN standards, with banned-user labels for dynamic node classification), and anonymized transaction banks such as Elliptic. Variants: CAWN (attention by causal walks), compressed memorization; the state-of-the-art survey lives on the temporal graph learning side. A TGN detector under attack and drift is the core of the end-of-year project [Y2.5](../../projects/index.html#y2-5), which reuses exercises 8 and 9.
:::

## 7. Robustness and privacy on graphs {#ch7}

Graph models are exposed to attackers who can add or remove a few edges, and graph data often reveals private information. This chapter studies attacks at test and training time, defenses and certification, then privacy and fairness on graphs.

::: thm
[7.1 — Nettack (Zügner, Akbarnejad & Günnemann, 2018): greedy search on a linearized surrogate]{.tag} The scenario: a target node $u$ and its class $y_u$; budget: $\Delta$ modifications (edge additions/removals, feature changes), applied at test time (*evasion*) or before retraining (*poisoning*) — the paper reports both. The attacker's dilemma: the model is not differentiable *in* the discrete structure. Nettack's solution, the one summarized in [Security, Case study 9.2](../m2-security-robustness/index.html#ch9):

1.  train a linearized *surrogate*: a two-layer GCN without its nonlinearity, whose logits are
    $$
    \hat A^2 X W ;
    $$
2.  **exact score** of each candidate (flip of an edge, or of a feature): the surrogate margin of the target *after* the flip,
    $$
    \mathcal{L}_s = \max_{c \neq y_u} \big[\hat A^2 X W\big]_{uc} - \big[\hat A^2 X W\big]_{u y_u} .
    $$
    For an edge, one flip changes only a few entries of $\hat A^2$, which are updated incrementally in constant time. For a feature, the margin is linear in $X$, so its gradient gives the exact score;
3.  greedily apply the best candidate and repeat until the budget is spent. *Unnoticeability* constraints keep the attack discreet: the perturbed degree distribution must pass a likelihood-ratio test against the clean one, and added features must co-occur plausibly with existing ones.

Gradient-based structure attacks exist too — FGA (Chen et al., 2018) ranks edges by the gradient of the loss with respect to $A$, and Metattack (7.2) uses meta-gradients — but Nettack scores discrete flips exactly.

Historic result: a few flips suffice to flip the prediction — and the attacks *transfer* to the true GCN (the surrogate suffices). The LLGA lesson: in fraud detection, the attacker *knows* the model (or its shadow); robustness is a design requirement, not an option.
:::

::: thm
[7.2 — Poisoning: Metattack (Zügner & Günnemann, 2019)]{.tag} An attack *at training time* (poisoning): the graph is corrupted *before* learning. Bilevel:
$$
\min_{\delta}\ \mathcal{L}_{atk}\big(f_{\theta^*}(A + \delta)\big) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \theta^* = \arg\min_\theta \mathcal{L}_{train}\big(f_\theta(A + \delta)\big),
$$
solved by *meta-gradient*: a few inner gradient steps are unrolled (differentiable), and the outer gradient flows back to $\delta$.

**MAML in three lines** (Finn, Abbeel & Levine, 2017). Model-agnostic meta-learning learns an initialization $\theta$ such that one or a few gradient steps on a new task,
$$
\theta' = \theta - \eta \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{task}(\theta),
$$
already perform well. Its outer gradient differentiates *through* these inner steps. Metattack uses the same unrolled differentiation, with respect to the graph instead of the initialization.

The attack loss needs labels that the attacker does not have on unlabeled nodes. **Meta-Self** trains a surrogate on the labeled nodes, takes its *predicted* labels on the unlabeled ones (self-training) and sets $\mathcal{L}_{atk} = -\mathcal{L}_{self}$, the negated loss on these pseudo-labels; **Meta-Train** uses $-\mathcal{L}_{train}$ instead. In both, the attacker controls no label — only the graph.

Structural defenses:

-   **pruning** (attack edges are often "suspicious" — large feature distances);
-   **purification** (Pro-GNN: learn a clean graph $A'$ regularized close to $A$ while training the GNN);
-   **robust GCN** (RGCN, Zhu, Zhang, Cui & Zhu, KDD 2019): Gaussian layers whose variance absorbs the attack + attention over reliable neighbors.
:::

::: note
[7.3 — Certification: sketch]{.tag} Guarantee that no attack of budget $\Delta$ changes the prediction: by *randomized smoothing* applied to graphs (majority over graphs perturbed by random flips, as in [Security ch. 5](../m2-security-robustness/index.html#ch5)) or by convex relaxations of the network (Zügner & Günnemann, KDD 2019, for feature perturbations, with a robust training that enlarges the certified set). The state of the art certifies small budgets on moderate GCNs: in practice, one combines partial certification + the defenses above + monitoring (detecting edge-addition anomalies).
:::

::: thm
[7.4 — Privacy: node-DP, edge-DP, reidentification]{.tag}

-   **edge-DP**: the basic mechanism is *randomized response* on the adjacency matrix — each pair of nodes is reported truthfully with probability $p > \frac12$ and flipped otherwise. This is $\varepsilon$-edge-DP with
    $$
    \varepsilon = \ln \frac{p}{1 - p} ,
    $$
    the convention of [Privacy & UQ, Proposition 4.2](../m2-privacy-uncertainty/index.html#ch4) (exercise 10). With a trusted curator, a counting query (how many edges between two groups?) can instead receive Laplace noise of sensitivity 1;
-   **node-DP**: much harder — sensitivity explodes with the degree (removing a node removes $d$ edges); recipe: *project* the graph onto a graph of bounded degree $k$ (keep the $k$ "most important" neighbors), then apply the edge mechanisms; the price: bias on hubs;
-   **reidentification**: graph embeddings (M1, ch. 3) are fingerprints — re-routing an "anonymized" node into a public graph by comparing neighborhoods (attacks by degrees, by subgraphs — the Narayanan-Shmatikov attack transposed); GraphRAG (M1, ch. 10) aggregates scattered facts: the reidentification risk *grows* with the quality of the graph;
-   **evaluation**: measure the utility-privacy trade-off (AUC vs $\varepsilon$); cross-reference with the M2 security module for LLMs (prompt injection over the KG, leakage by generation).
:::

::: note
[7.5 — Structural fairness]{.tag} Degree bias: low-degree nodes (minorities in social networks, new customers) are predicted less well — fewer messages = less signal; remedies: structural features (RWSE, ch. 4), virtual edges, degree-based resampling, reweighted losses; open question: *structural* fairness (communities) vs *individual* fairness (nodes) can conflict — the exact counterpart of the fairness tensions of the Optimal Transport module (transporting node distributions; homophily bias: a homophilous GNN propagates label biases).
:::

## 8. LLGA bridges: 3D, algorithmic reasoning, GNN × LLM {#ch8}

This chapter connects the module to the other axes of the master: geometric graphs (3D molecules), GNNs that learn to execute algorithms, and the combination of GNNs with LLMs.

::: thm
[8.1 — 3D molecules: EGNN and E(n) equivariance (Satorras, Hoogeboom & Welling, 2021)]{.tag} The positions $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$ make the molecular graph *geometric*; physics is invariant under rotations/translations (E(3)); a GNN that respects this symmetry *by construction* learns better with less data (Bronstein et al., the Geometric DL "charter").

**Recall.** The EGNN layer and the proof of its E(n)-equivariance are in [Graph ML, Proposition 8.3](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch8). In short, the messages read only invariant distances,
$$
m_{ij} = \phi_e\big(h_i, h_j, \|x_i - x_j\|^2, e_{ij}\big),
$$
and each position moves along the differences $x_i - x_j$, weighted by $\phi_x(m_{ij})$. Under $x \mapsto Qx + t$ with $Q$ orthogonal, the features are unchanged and the positions follow.

What this module adds:

-   *applications*: 3D property prediction (invariant features into a readout) and learned molecular dynamics (equivariant outputs as forces);
-   *the bridge to diffusion*: an EGNN is the denoiser of equivariant diffusion models — EDM (Hoogeboom et al., ICML 2022) generates atom types and coordinates jointly, GeoDiff (Xu et al., ICLR 2022) generates the conformers (3D coordinates) of a given molecular graph. With an equivariant denoiser, an isotropic prior and centered coordinates, the learned density is invariant to rotations and translations;
-   the M2 Geometric DL module generalizes to groups; M1 ch. 9 covers the 2D version, and [Graph Generative Models](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html) takes over the generation side.
:::

::: thm
[8.2 — Neural algorithmic reasoning (Veličković et al.)]{.tag} Learning to *execute* algorithms with GNNs: encode inputs as a graph (sorting: a list = a comparison graph; shortest paths: the graph itself), execute via message passing layers, decode outputs — the *black-box* replaces the code.

The CLRS benchmark (Veličković et al., ICML 2022) tests faithful execution of classical algorithms (CLRS = Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein). Results: GNN processors generalize to unseen sizes *better* than transformers on certain families (structural induction).

The LLGA lesson: a learned algorithm is *differentiable* (it can be inserted into an end-to-end trained pipeline: routing, scheduling, matching) and *approximately robust* (noisy inputs); at the price of exactness — the trade-off to master.

Routing is the natural target: shortest paths and minimum spanning trees are CLRS tasks, and the end-of-year project [Y2.4](../../projects/index.html#y2-4) puts a learned router next to an exact solver.

Loop with Refresher CS: what more can a "learned algorithm" do than an algorithm? Answer: train on data, slot into gradient descent — and the pseudo-code prompting of ch. 9.4 is the dual path (the LLM *simulates* the execution; NAR *embodies* it).
:::

::: thm
[8.3 — GNN × LLM: injected encoders, alignment and benchmarks]{.tag} Three injection architectures. The site-wide taxonomy is the one of [Graph ML 10.2](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10) (soft tokens, structural recall, cross-distillation); the table maps the names used here onto it.

| Architecture (here) | Graph ML 10.2 | What is trained | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **structural tokens**: GNN outputs projected into the LLM's embedding space; the LLM reads structure as a language | (a) soft tokens | the projector (and the GNN); LLM frozen or LoRA | GraphGPT (Tang et al., SIGIR 2024), G-Retriever (He et al., NeurIPS 2024) |
| **structural recall**: the GNN or a graph traversal retrieves the relevant facts, the LLM writes — "graph-RAG" | (b) structural recall | the retriever | GraphRAG (Graph ML 10.1), the subgraph retrieval of G-Retriever |
| **LLM annotator**: the LLM enriches node features (summaries, explanations, types) for the GNN — the text-attributed graph ("TAG") regime | (c) cross-distillation, LLM → GNN direction | the GNN, on the LLM-enriched features | TAPE (He et al., ICLR 2024) on ogbn-arxiv |

**Worked: soft tokens.** A node $v$, or each node of a small retrieved subgraph, is encoded by a GNN into $z_v \in \mathbb{R}^{d_g}$. A two-layer MLP projector maps it to the width $d_{\mathrm{LLM}}$ of the LLM's token embeddings:
$$
t_v = W_2\, \mathrm{GELU}(W_1 z_v) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{LLM}}} .
$$
The vectors $t_v$ are inserted before the embeddings of the prompt tokens, as if they were extra words. The LLM stays frozen (or LoRA-adapted, [LLM 4.3](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#peft)); the projector, and possibly the GNN, are trained with the next-token loss on the answer tokens only.

Sizes: with $d_g = 256$, a hidden width of 1,024 and $d_{\mathrm{LLM}} = 2{,}048$ (a 1B-parameter LLM), the projector has about 2.4M parameters — negligible next to the LLM.

**Worked: graph–text alignment.** Soft tokens work better when the two spaces already agree. Take a batch of $B$ nodes with GNN embeddings $z_i$ and text embeddings $c_i$ of their descriptions (title and abstract of a paper, for instance). Two linear heads map them to a common space, normalized to unit length:
$$
a_i = \frac{W_g z_i}{\|W_g z_i\|}, \qquad b_j = \frac{W_t c_j}{\|W_t c_j\|}, \qquad s_{ij} = \frac{\langle a_i, b_j \rangle}{\tau},
$$
with a temperature $\tau$. The **symmetric InfoNCE** loss, as in CLIP, treats each matching pair as the positive and the other $B - 1$ items of the batch as negatives, in both directions:
$$
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2B} \sum_{i=1}^{B} \Big[ \log \frac{e^{s_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{s_{ij}}} + \log \frac{e^{s_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{s_{ji}}} \Big] .
$$

*By hand*, with $B = 2$ and the score matrix
$$
S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0.5 & 1.5 \end{pmatrix} :
$$

-   graph → text (rows): $\log(1 + e^{-2}) = 0.127$ and $\log(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.313$;
-   text → graph (columns): $\log(1 + e^{-1.5}) = 0.201$ twice;
-   hence
    $$
    \mathcal{L} = \frac{0.127 + 0.313 + 0.201 + 0.201}{4} \approx 0.211 .
    $$

The loss falls as the diagonal dominates each row *and* each column. After alignment, a node can be retrieved from a text query and the reverse, and zero-shot classification works by matching a node with the texts of the class names. Exercise 11 runs this on ogbn-arxiv.

Benchmarks: NLGraph (serialized reasoning — M1, ch. 10.2), Talk like a Graph (encodings: none dominates everywhere), and the industrial GraphRAG suites.

**Industrial GraphRAG** (summary; details in M1, ch. 10): LLM extraction → entity graph → Leiden communities + summaries → local/global queries; the M2's role: the *quality of the graph* (robust communities — ch. 7; KGC completion — M1 ch. 6) is the system's bottleneck; the rare specialty the master builds: both GNN theory *and* the LLM pipeline. The GNN retriever and the graph tokens of this section are two options of the end-of-year project [Y2.1](../../projects/index.html#y2-1) (biomedical question answering on STaRK-Prime).
:::

::: note
[8.4 — What the master expects of you here]{.tag} Knowing how to choose: MPNN vs transformer (ch. 5), with or without PE (ch. 4), deep or rewired (ch. 3), certified or not (ch. 7) — and knowing how to *prove* the theorems of ch. 2, reproduce the experiments of ch. 9, and read a paper of the field in one hour. This is the "entry-level research / advanced R&D" level.
:::

## 9. Research at DaSciM (Vazirgiannis, Lutzeyer) {#ch9}

The DaSciM laboratory (LIX, École Polytechnique — M. Vazirgiannis, J. Lutzeyer) is the master's host laboratory: this chapter studies its papers in depth, positioning them *relative to the program*. General-audience introductions were given in M1 (ch. 11); here we go into the machinery.

::: thm
[9.1 — Path Neural Networks, in depth (Michel, Nikolentzos, Lutzeyer & Vazirgiannis, ICML 2023)]{.tag} **Starting point**: the canonical GNN layer aggregates 1-hop neighbors (M1, ch. 5); stacking $L$ layers amounts — when all goes well — to aggregating *walks* of length $L$. But

1.  walks *repeat* nodes (backtracking — redundant information);
2.  composing layers degrades (over-smoothing/squashing, ch. 3);
3.  1-WL — hence the GNN (th. 2.2) — aggregates only multisets of colors, without the *sequence* of the route.

**The path operator**: for each node $v$ and each length $\ell \leq K$, take a collection $\mathcal{P}_v^{(\ell)}$ of *simple* paths (without repeated nodes) of length $\ell$ starting from $v$. Each path is encoded by an LSTM run over the node representations along it, ending at $v$, and the codes are summed:
$$
m_p = \mathrm{LSTM}\big(h_{u_\ell}^{(\ell-1)}, \dots, h_{u_1}^{(\ell-1)}, h_v^{(\ell-1)}\big), \qquad h_v^{(\ell)} = \mathrm{COMBINE}\Big(h_v^{(\ell-1)}, \sum_{p \in \mathcal{P}_v^{(\ell)}} m_p\Big).
$$
Three variants choose the collection of paths, each contained in the next (SP ⊆ SP+ ⊆ AP):

-   **PathNN-SP**: a *single* shortest path for each pair of nodes — captures *distances*: two nodes "close to everyone" versus "peripheral" separate;
-   **PathNN-SP+**: *all* shortest paths between each pair — also counts how many geodesics join two nodes;
-   **PathNN-AP**: *all simple paths* of length up to $K$ — the most expressive and the most expensive, so $K$ stays small (5 in the paper's synthetic experiments).

There is no random-walk variant: the point of the operator is to use paths that, unlike walks, repeat no node (problem 1 above).

**Complexity**: $\mathcal{O}(P \cdot K \cdot d^2)$ per node for $P$ paths of length at most $K$ — of the same order as a GAT if $P \sim \bar d$. For AP, $P$ grows exponentially with $K$ in dense graphs.

**Results**: on graph classification and regression — six TU datasets (DD, NCI1, PROTEINS, ENZYMES, IMDB-B, IMDB-M, with the 10-fold protocol of Errica et al., 2020), ogbg-molhiv, ZINC12K, Peptides-func and Peptides-struct — PathNN matches or exceeds GIN/GCN in most cases; on tasks where *the geometry of routes* carries the signal (molecules: paths are chemical chains!), the gain is clear.

**Theoretical positioning**: the paper proves that PathNN-SP+ and PathNN-AP are strictly more powerful than 1-WL, and PathNN-AP even separates strongly regular graphs that 3-WL confuses. Simple paths carry information that walk multisets ignore. Recall C6 vs 2×C3 (Example 2.4): a node of 2×C3 has no simple path of length 3, since its component has three nodes, while a node of C6 has two. Ordered recurrent aggregation is also the tool of GOAT (below), and PathNN is the subject of the "paper" exercise (exercise 12).
:::

::: thm
[9.2 — GOAT (Chatzianastasis, Lutzeyer, Dasoulas & Vazirgiannis, AAAI 2023)]{.tag} Introduced in M1 (ch. 11.3), which also links its learned order to the node-ordering problem of autoregressive graph generation. GOAT itself is not a generative model: it learns node representations, and here we study its expressive power. The invariant aggregator $\mathrm{AGG}$ (th. 2.2–2.3) bounds the GNN to 1-WL *precisely because it is invariant*.

GOAT learns a **local order** by attention (scoring neighbors by $(h_v, h_u)$, sorting), then processes the sequence with an RNN — a sequence model *inside* the graph. It is strictly more expressive than invariant aggregation (it distinguishes identical distributions of a multiset as soon as the order carries signal), while remaining *globally* equivariant (the order is a learned function of the representations, not an external numbering).

Positioning in M2: an *architectural* answer to the question of ch. 2 — gain expressive power without paying $\mathcal{O}(n^k)$; and an answer to ch. 4 — the local order is a *learned* positional encoding.
:::

::: thm
[9.3 — NGG (Evdaimon et al., 2024): conditioned latent generation]{.tag} The bridge M1-ch. 9 ↔ diffusion: a GNN encoder projects graphs into a compact latent space; a diffusion model (M1, ch. 9.5 — Multimodal GenAI) learns the distribution there *conditioned on structural features* (spectrum, degrees, counts); the decoder regenerates graphs exhibiting the requested features.

The interest for M2: *latent* diffusion bypasses discretization (continuous diffusion in $\mathbb{R}^d$ rather than over DiGress's categories), and the spectral conditioning connects generation to ch. 3 (the spectrum governs communication — here, it governs the *shape* of the generated graphs). LLGA applications: faithful synthetic data (pre-training!), distributional anonymization, anomaly detection (a real graph far from the latent support).
:::

::: note
[9.4 — Pseudo-code prompting (Skianis, Nikolentzos & Vazirgiannis, 2024)]{.tag} Presented in M1 (ch. 10) as a GraphRAG tool; the M2 reading: a benchmark of *algorithmic reasoning* — LLMs execute graphs described in pseudo-code better than in natural language (systematic gains); to be connected with neural algorithmic reasoning (ch. 8): two ways of making algorithms run on graphs — by a prompted LLM, or by a trained GNN.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ 1-WL by hand.** Run 1-WL on C6 and 2×C3 and verify indistinguishability (detail Example 2.4); then on the "house" graph (square + roof) versus the pentagon; conclude on the exact family of indistinguishable pairs.

    *Partial solution*: the house has degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 2 — the two eaves, where the roof meets the square, have degree 3, and the roof top has degree 2 (an even number of odd degrees, as the handshake lemma requires). The pentagon is 2-regular, so 1-WL distinguishes them from iteration 1 (initial color = degree).

    Generalization: 1-WL confuses *every* pair of $d$-regular graphs with the same number of nodes, since all colors stay equal — for instance all unions of cycles with the same total number of nodes. It also confuses non-regular pairs: two graphs are 1-WL-equivalent exactly when they admit equitable partitions with the same cell sizes and the same numbers of neighbors between cells (fractional isomorphism: Tinhofer, 1986; Ramana, Scheinerman & Ullman, 1994).
2.  **★ LapEig.** Compute the first 2 nontrivial eigenvectors of the Laplacian of the karate club graph; project the nodes; verify that the visualized separation ≈ the actual partition; rerun 5 times and observe the sign flips; implement the SignNet correction (ch. 4.1) and measure stability (distance between the encodings of two runs).

    *Partial solution*: $\rho\big([\phi(v_i) + \phi(-v_i)]_{i}\big)$ with MLPs $\phi, \rho$ — each even term is invariant under the flip of its eigenvector; compare with the baseline "sign fixed by the first positive component" (unstable at nodes of near-zero value).
3.  **★ RWSE by hand and in code.** Recover the computations of Example 4.2 (triangle vs hexagon), then compute the RWSEs ($K = 4$) of all nodes of the karate club graph. Show that two nodes exchanged by an automorphism always get the same RWSE. Then take the 2-regular graph C3 ∪ C6 (disjoint union), where all nodes are 1-WL-equivalent, and show that RWSE separates the triangle's nodes from the hexagon's. Explain why automorphism invariance is both a *feature* (the encoding does not depend on the numbering) and a *limit* (no such encoding separates automorphic nodes, even when a task needs it).

    *Partial solution*: let $\Pi$ be the permutation matrix of an automorphism $\sigma$. Then
    $$
    \Pi A \Pi^\top = A, \quad \text{so} \quad \Pi P^k \Pi^\top = P^k \quad \text{and} \quad (P^k)_{\sigma(v)\sigma(v)} = (P^k)_{vv} .
    $$
    In C3 ∪ C6, $(P^3)_{vv} = \frac14$ on the triangle and $0$ on the hexagon.
4.  **★★ GIN vs GCN.** Show that the mean is not injective on multisets (give the counterexamples {a, a, a} vs {a} and {a, a, b, b} vs {a, b}) and that sum+MLP is (discrete features); check experimentally: train GIN and GCN on a 1-WL-indistinguishable pair and measure.

    *Partial solution*: mean: {a, a, a} → a and {a} → a (collision); discrete sum: encode a by $\log 2$, b by $\log 3$ — $\{a,a,b,b\} \mapsto 2\log 2 + 2\log 3 = \log 36$ and $\{a, b\} \mapsto \log 6$ — no collision by uniqueness of factorization (th. 2.3); in practice, the mean does better on continuous real features — discuss why (estimation variance).
5.  **★★ Minimal pair GNN.** Implement a pair GNN with the folklore rule of Example 2.4: a representation $h_{uv}$ per pair, updated from the multiset of $(h_{uw}, h_{wv})$ over all $w$. Verify that it separates C6 and 2×C3 (disjoint readout outputs) where GIN fails. Then implement the 2-WL rule (two separate multisets) and check that it fails, as the k-WL box predicts.

    *Hint*: start with hashed colors (exact 2-FWL and 2-WL) before learning. With dense tensors, the sum over $w$ of $h_{uw} \odot h_{wv}$ is one matrix product per channel — the trick of PPGN.
6.  **★★ Over-squashing.** Build two "communities" connected by a single bottleneck node; measure the classification performance of a GCN as a function of the distance to the bottleneck; compare GPS (ch. 5), GCN + SDRF and GCN + DIGL. Plot the spectral gap $\lambda_2$ of $L_{\mathrm{sym}}$ (or the effective resistance between the two sides) before and after rewiring, with the Jacobian sensitivity of Definition 3.1 computed by autograd.

    *Partial solution (expected)*: gradient of accuracy with distance for the GCN; GPS nearly uniform. With two random communities of 30 nodes (edge probability 0.3), three edges added across the bottleneck raise $\lambda_2$ from about 0.003 to about 0.02. DIGL (PPR with teleport 0.15, top-8 per node) only reaches about 0.005, as Theorem 6 of Topping et al. predicts.

    The effective resistance
    $$
    R_{uv} = (e_u - e_v)^\top L^{+} (e_u - e_v)
    $$
    across the bottleneck falls accordingly (Black et al., 2023); the curve of accuracy against $\lambda_2$ is the graph to produce.
7.  **★★ Graphormer-PE.** Implement the attention bias by shortest-path distance (distance matrix by BFS; learned bias table — skeleton in ch. 5.1); train on ogbg-molhiv and compare GCN / GIN / Graphormer-mini; report means ± standard deviations over 5 seeds.

    *Partial solution*: BFS $\mathcal{O}(n(|V| + |E|))$ per graph — precompute; clamp distances at a `max_spd` read from the distance histogram of the training molecules, with a separate slot for unreachable pairs (code of 5.1); expected: a small but systematic gain of the SPD bias over GCN.
8.  **★★ Temporal.** On a standard TGN dataset (Wikipedia/Reddit): train a TGN (`torch_geometric.nn.models.TGNMemory` from PyTorch Geometric, or the paper's code); ablation: remove memory (keep the TGAT embedding); plot the AUC of future link prediction as a function of the horizon $\Delta t$.

    *Partial solution (expected)*: memory dominates on recent interactions; without memory, the AUC drops by several points at small $\Delta t$ (the information of the last events is no longer compressed).
9.  **★★ Attack.** Implement a Nettack-style structure attack on a target node (ch. 7.1): train the linearized two-layer surrogate, score every candidate edge flip by the exact surrogate margin after the flip, apply the best one and repeat $k$ times. Measure the prediction flip rate of a normally trained GCN against the budget $k$; test a defense (RGCN or training on perturbed graphs).

    *Partial solution*: with $\hat A^2$ updated incrementally, each candidate is cheap to score. Compare with the gradient ranking of FGA (magnitude of the gradient of the attack loss per candidate edge), cheaper but only a first-order approximation of the same choice. The surrogate suffices (transfer). A defense raises the budget needed to flip a target but makes no target immune; conclude on certification (ch. 7.3).
10. **★★ Edge-DP.** Prove that randomized response — each pair of nodes reported truthfully with probability $p > \tfrac12$, flipped otherwise — is $(\varepsilon, 0)$-edge-DP with $\varepsilon = \ln \frac{p}{1-p}$ (the convention of Privacy & UQ, Proposition 4.2). Then estimate the number of edges between two groups from the released graph, and compare its error with the Laplace mechanism applied to the true count by a trusted curator.

    *Solution*: for two graphs neighboring in one edge, all other pairs have the same output law, and the differing pair is reported present with probability $p$ in one graph and $1-p$ in the other. The likelihood ratio of any output is therefore at most $\frac{p}{1-p}$, hence the $\varepsilon$.

    Counting: over the $m$ pairs between the two groups, with $c$ true edges, the released count $S$ has mean
    $$
    \mathbb{E}[S] = c\,p + (m - c)(1 - p) = m(1 - p) + (2p - 1)\,c ,
    $$
    so $\hat c = \big(S - m(1-p)\big)/(2p - 1)$ is unbiased, with variance
    $$
    \mathrm{Var}(\hat c) = \frac{m\, p(1-p)}{(2p-1)^2} .
    $$

    The Laplace mechanism on the true count (sensitivity 1, scale $1/\varepsilon$) has variance $2/\varepsilon^2$, independent of $m$. With $p = 0.75$, $\varepsilon = \ln 3 \approx 1.10$ and $m = 1000$ pairs, the standard deviations are about 27 edges for randomized response and 1.3 for Laplace: local noise is the price of not trusting a curator.
11. **★★ Aligning a GNN with a text encoder on ogbn-arxiv.** On ogbn-arxiv (169,343 papers, 40 subject classes; titles and abstracts from the OGB mapping to MAG), train a 2-layer GraphSAGE and embed each title with a frozen sentence encoder. Train two linear heads with the symmetric InfoNCE loss of 8.3 (batches of 512, learned $\tau$). Report:

    -   (a) graph → text recall@10 among 1,000 random test candidates;
    -   (b) zero-shot node classification by cosine similarity with the embedded names of the 40 classes, against a GraphSAGE trained with labels;
    -   (c) optionally, one soft token per node in a small open LLM, with the projector trained to generate the class name.

    *Partial solution (expected)*: chance level is 1 % for (a) (10 out of 1,000) and 2.5 % for (b) (1 out of 40); the aligned model should be far above both, and (b) below supervised training. Expect most zero-shot confusions between neighboring fields. Map your pipeline onto the table of 8.3: (a)–(b) align the spaces, (c) is the soft-token architecture.
12. **★★★ Research project.** Reproduce an experiment from one of (PathNN / GOAT / GPS / TGN / NGG) on OGB or TU; report: protocol, seeds, comparison to the published numbers, failure analysis — the M2's "paper" exercise; for PathNN: compare the three variants (SP / SP+ / AP) on a molecular dataset (ZINC12K) and explain the observed hierarchy via ch. 9.1.

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The fiche above records that the SynapseS 2026–2027 sheet of this module is "not published": the module appears in neither the S3 nor the S4 track of the catalog, so no official assessment is displayed. Everything below is a proposal of these notes, not an official rule. The subjects are sized for an M2 module and reuse the experimental protocol of ch. 1 (seeds, confidence intervals, leakage checks), which every rubric line assumes.

The projects exercise mainly O4 (graph-structured data: expressive power, over-squashing, encodings, temporal graphs), O5 (Graph × LLM: soft tokens, alignment, graph prompting) and O8 (robustness and privacy on graphs), with O7 (hands-on, reproducible research practice). They feed the end-of-year projects [Y2.1](../../projects/index.html#y2-1), [Y2.4](../../projects/index.html#y2-4) and [Y2.5](../../projects/index.html#y2-5).

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] A test bench for expressive power.** Which models separate which hard pairs of graphs, and does every outcome match a statement of ch. 2 and ch. 4?
    -   *Work*: implement 1-WL, 2-WL and 2-FWL by hashing, GCN, GIN, an ego-net subgraph GNN in the style of ESAN, and GIN with RWSE or LapEig + SignNet inputs.
    -   *Data*: synthetic pairs built with NetworkX — C6 vs 2×C3, house vs pentagon, the $4 \times 4$ rook's graph vs the Shrikhande graph (both strongly regular with parameters (16, 6, 2, 2)) — and the CSL graphs of Murphy et al. (ICML 2019), 41-node 4-regular cycles with skip links, in 10 classes.
    -   *Success criterion*: a models × pairs table in which each entry is predicted, before running, by a result of the page — including the negative ones: 2-FWL and RWSE must both fail on the strongly regular pair.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, a 4–6 page report, a 10-minute talk; chapters 2 and 4, exercises 1, 3 and 5.
2.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Paper study: Path Neural Networks (Michel, Nikolentzos, Lutzeyer & Vazirgiannis, ICML 2023).** Do the three variants rank as their theory says, on synthetic pairs and on real benchmarks?
    -   *Work*: reimplement PathNN-SP, SP+ and AP (path enumeration up to length $K$, LSTM path encoder of 9.1); check the separation claims on the pairs of solo project 1; then train on ZINC12K and two TU datasets.
    -   *Data*: ZINC12K (Dwivedi et al.'s benchmarking subset) and PROTEINS and IMDB-B from TUDataset, with the 10-fold splits of Errica et al. (2020).
    -   *Success criterion*: published numbers reproduced within one standard deviation, or the gap explained (budget, splits, $K$); the SP ≤ SP+ ≤ AP ordering tested, with its cost in time and memory.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, report, talk; chapters 2 and 9, extending exercise 12.

### Group projects {#projects-group}

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Diagnosing and curing over-squashing.** Do rewiring, deep propagation and global attention fix the long-range failures that the bound of Definition 3.1 predicts?
    -   *Work*: measure the Jacobian sensitivity by autograd against distance, the spectral gap $\lambda_2$, the effective resistance and the edge curvatures; then compare SDRF, DIGL, APPNP, GCNII, GPS and Exphormer under one parameter budget.
    -   *Data*: synthetic barbell graphs and the Tree-NeighborsMatch task of Alon & Yahav (2021), depths 2–6; then Peptides-func from the Long Range Graph Benchmark (Dwivedi et al., NeurIPS 2022), with its budget of about 500k parameters.
    -   *Split*: diagnostics and rewiring; deep MPNNs; graph transformers — with one shared training harness.
    -   *Success criterion*: average precision on Peptides-func with 95 % intervals over 5 seeds; $\lambda_2$ before and after each rewiring; a decision guide that confirms or corrects 5.4.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, an 8–10 page joint report, a 20-minute talk; chapters 1, 3 and 5.
2.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Abuse detection on an event stream, under attack and under privacy.** How much do memory, a budgeted attacker and an edge-DP release each cost a temporal detector?
    -   *Work*: TGN and TGAT for dynamic node classification with a chronological 70/15/15 split; the memory ablation of exercise 8; an evasion attack that injects $k$ events from attacker-controlled accounts, and a pruning or RGCN-style defense; a release of the training graph by randomized response (7.4) at several $\varepsilon$.
    -   *Data*: the Wikipedia and Reddit interaction streams of JODIE (Kumar, Zhang & Leskovec, KDD 2019), with their banned-user labels; for a finance variant, the Elliptic Bitcoin graph (Weber et al., 2019) with snapshot models.
    -   *Split*: temporal models and leakage checks; attack and defense; privacy release and evaluation.
    -   *Success criterion*: AUC against attack budget and against $\varepsilon$, with intervals over 5 seeds; the leakage checklist of [Graph ML 5.6–5.8](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch5) passed.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, joint report, talk; chapters 1, 6 and 7, exercises 8–10. It is a first version of [Y2.5](../../projects/index.html#y2-5) and links to [Security ch. 9](../m2-security-robustness/index.html#ch9) and [Privacy & UQ ch. 4](../m2-privacy-uncertainty/index.html#ch4).
3.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Graph tokens for an LLM.** For a small open LLM, which input answers graph-reasoning questions best as graphs grow: text, pseudo-code or soft tokens?
    -   *Work*: three pipelines on the same questions — text serialization with the encodings of Talk like a Graph (Fatemi, Halcrow & Perozzi, ICLR 2024); pseudo-code prompting (Skianis, Nikolentzos & Vazirgiannis, 2024; 9.4); and a GPS + RWSE encoder whose outputs enter the LLM as soft tokens, after the symmetric InfoNCE alignment of 8.3, with LoRA on the LLM.
    -   *Data*: synthetic questions in the style of GraphQA (edge existence, degree, cycle check, connectivity, shortest path) on random graphs of 5 to 50 nodes, and the NLGraph benchmark (Wang et al., NeurIPS 2023); a model of 0.5B to 1.5B parameters on a free GPU.
    -   *Split*: prompting pipelines; encoder, projector and alignment; evaluation harness and size curves.
    -   *Success criterion*: accuracy against the number of nodes for each task and pipeline, with intervals over 3 seeds and an equal training-data budget for the trained pipelines.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, joint report, talk; chapters 4, 5, 8 and 9. It connects to [LLM 4.3](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#peft) (LoRA) and [LLM ch. 7](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#ch7) (retrieval), to [Graph ML 10.2](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch10), and is the graph-token option of [Y2.1](../../projects/index.html#y2-1).
